opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's made me a lot more humble about it. When we wrote the paper, I don't think any of us expected that, years later, essentially the same architecture would still be the backbone of almost everything. If you'd asked me back then, I probably would have guessed something better would come along within a couple of years. That just hasn't happened.

So I've basically stopped making those predictions. Part of it is that the Transformer turned out to be a really good fit for the hardware we have. It's extremely parallelizable, it maps well onto GPUs and accelerators, and the whole ecosystem has co-evolved around it: the kernels, the compilers, the training recipes, the inference stacks. Any new architecture isn't just competing with the Transformer as an idea. It's competing with years of optimization layered on top of it. That's a very high bar.

The other part is that the Transformer has been surprisingly flexible. A lot of what people propose as replacements ends up getting absorbed: better attention variants, mixture-of-experts, state-space-style ideas mixed in, longer context tricks. The thing keeps evolving without really being displaced.

I do think something will eventually replace it. There's no reason to believe we stumbled onto the final answer. But I'd be skeptical of anyone who gives you a confident date. What I'd watch for is an architecture that offers a step change, not a marginal gain, on something that really matters, like efficiency at long context or the ability to learn continuously. Small wins won't be enough to overcome the inertia. It'll take something that's obviously, dramatically better, and right now I can't tell you when that shows up.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he expected something better to arrive within a couple of years, but does not specify 2018, near-zero probability, or seven years later.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the Transformer’s longevity made him more humble and that he has basically stopped predicting when it will be replaced.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's made me a lot more humble. When we wrote the paper in 2017, I think most of us assumed it would be a stepping stone, that something would come along in two or three years and eclipse it the way it eclipsed LSTMs. And every year since, I've had people ask me, "What's next? What replaces the Transformer?" And for a long time I'd confidently say, "Oh, something's coming, give it eighteen months." I've been wrong about that repeatedly, so I've stopped putting dates on it.

What I underestimated was how much the architecture benefits from a kind of compounding lock-in. It's not just that attention is a good idea. It's that the entire hardware stack got optimized around it, the software tooling got optimized around it, the research community built intuitions around it, and then scaling laws told everyone that the fastest path to better models was more data and more compute on the same architecture rather than a fundamentally new one. So even when something comes along that looks genuinely better in a paper, state space models, various linear attention schemes, mixtures of experts, which is really more of a modification, it has to overcome years of accumulated optimization just to be competitive. That's a very high bar.

So my view now is that it probably won't be a clean replacement. It'll be erosion. You'll see pieces swapped out, attention variants that are cheaper at long context, hybrid layers, different training objectives, and at some point you'll look back and realize the thing you're running doesn't look much like the 2017 model even though nobody ever declared a successor. If you forced me to guess, I'd say the "Transformer" name sticks around far longer than the actual architecture does.

And I'd add that I think the bigger shifts are going to come from what you do with the model rather than the model itself. How you train it, what data you feed it, how it interacts with tools and acts in the world, how you do inference-time compute. Those feel like they have more headroom right now than a new block diagram does. So I'm not predicting dates anymore. I'm just watching for the moment when the cost of staying on the current path exceeds the cost of switching, and I don't think we're there yet.

sol-6.1.text: It’s made me much more humble about making that prediction. I’ve thought a few times that we were probably nearing the end of the Transformer’s run, and it keeps surprising us. People keep finding ways to make it more efficient and push it further. So I’m reluctant to put a timeline on it now. I expect something will eventually replace it, but I don’t think we know when, or whether that will look like a completely new architecture or a gradual evolution of what we already have.
